=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of the Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

## 1. How the Seller has framed the package

Before the substance, the deal team should know how the Seller has presented this package.

- **The labels have no agreed status.** The Seller has marked most clauses "[STANDARD]", calls the package "FINAL… not intended to be re-opened", and says "both sides" have cleared the [STANDARD] items and "accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package". These are the Seller's own descriptions. Nothing I have shows that Wattlebridge agreed to any of them.
- **Please check with the principals.** If anyone on our side gave principal-level agreement on any of these terms, I need to know. If not, I suggest the reply states plainly that the labels are not accepted and that every clause remains open.
- **The "market context" preamble is partly accurate and partly not.** A 10–20% cap for general warranties in a deal this size is defensible. Buyer-knowledge exclusions, deductible baskets and capping title warranties at 20% are not standard buyer terms.
- **The Seller's own Disclosure Letter contradicts its "addressed" claims.** It confirms there is no Bluefen consent, Riverlark is not repaid, the bonuses are missing from the funds flow, and the incident is unresolved.

I reviewed every clause on its merits, including the ones marked [STANDARD]. The [STANDARD] items are where most of the risk sits.

*Caveat: I have only the Seller's summary of positions and the Disclosure Letter, not the full SPA text or the DD documents. Clause references are the Seller's. Points marked "verify" need checking against the source documents.*

## 2. The structural problem: the protections cancel each other out

Read together, four positions leave the Buyer with almost no recourse for the risks we already know about:

1. **General disclosure** of the whole data room and public records (Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2).
2. **Buyer-knowledge exclusion** covering anything "discoverable from the data room" (cl 8.3).
3. **Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance** applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5).
4. **Specific risks pushed into the general regime**: title, tax and IP all subject to the 20% cap and 18 months.

Every known issue (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the data incident, the bonuses, the Sandbar renewals) is in the data room. Under items 1 and 2, none of them could found a warranty claim. Under item 3, the Seller would argue we cannot sue on them any other way.

**The answer is to handle each known risk through conditions, completion mechanics, price deductions and specific indemnities, not warranties.** We should also reject items 1 to 4.

## 3. Issue-by-issue analysis

### A. Limitation package

| Clause | Seller position | Problem | Buyer position |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12.1 Cap | 20% (AUD 4.8m) for general warranties | Acceptable in range for general warranties only. Unacceptable if, via 12.3/13, it also covers title, tax, IP and indemnities. | Accept 20% (or seek 25–30%) for general warranties only. Fundamental, title and capacity warranties capped at 100% of price. Tax capped at 100%. Specific indemnities sit outside the general cap. Fraud is uncapped. |
| 12.2 Thresholds | AUD 25k de minimis; AUD 250k basket, **excess only** | A deductible basket means the Seller never pays the first AUD 250k. The bonus on-costs alone could fall inside it. | Tipping basket (once reached, recover from dollar one). De minimis around AUD 10–15k, with related claims aggregated. Neither threshold applies to fundamental, tax, specific indemnity, leakage or fraud claims. |
| 12.3/13 Time limits | 18 months, applied to **all** Claims "unless expressly stated otherwise" | The default rule catches title, tax, indemnities and covenants unless we spot and carve out each one. | 18 months for general warranties is acceptable. Title/capacity: 6–7 years. Tax: 7 years, or 60 days after the Commissioner's amendment period expires if later. Indemnities run to the limitation period for the underlying risk. Flip the default so limitations apply only where expressly stated. |
| Fundamental | Same cap and time as general warranties | Title is the asset being bought. 20% recovery on a title failure means we pay 24m and can recover 4.8m. | Reject outright. |

### B. Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5: limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature"

- **Fraud and dishonest concealment.** Limitations must not apply to these. Under NSW law a party generally cannot contract out of liability for its own fraud. Even so, the drafting should say this expressly so there is no argument.
- **Australian Consumer Law s 18.** Misleading or deceptive conduct liability cannot be excluded. However, non-reliance clauses carry evidentiary weight against a reliance case. Limit the non-reliance clause to statements outside the SPA, Disclosure Letter and warranties, and carve out fraud.
- **Exclusive remedy.** This must not cut across:
  - specific indemnities;
  - price adjustment or leakage claims;
  - covenant breaches (pre-completion conduct, restraints);
  - injunctive relief;
  - termination rights.

### C. Disclosure Letter and clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge)

**General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2): reject.** Our position should be:

- Only matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter qualify. Fairly disclosed means with enough detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter, against specific warranties.
- Data room documents are disclosed only if specifically referenced against a warranty. If anything is accepted, take a frozen, indexed copy on USB as an exhibit, not a moving data room.
- Public register disclosure is limited to searches conducted on a stated date, if conceded at all.
- **No disclosure against fundamental warranties or tax**, and none against specific indemnities.
- No updating of the disclosure between signing and completion, or any update gives the Buyer a termination right without curing the breach.

**Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3): reject.** Replace it with a clause stating that the Buyer's knowledge (actual, constructive or imputed), and the Buyer's investigation, do not reduce any claim. The Seller's wording ("the Buyer or its advisers", "discoverable") is especially wide. It would impute to Wattlebridge everything in every adviser's files and everything a search could find. If the Seller holds firm, the fallback is limiting it to the actual knowledge of named individuals, of matters fairly disclosed, as at signing.

**Disclosure Letter 1.4 and 11** (no admission; "Buyer must evaluate"). These are acceptable as reservation language. They also confirm the Seller is not standing behind its characterisations, such as "not expected to be material" and "ordinary course".

### D. Bluefen (DD-002): about AUD 3.6m revenue, around 30% of FY26

- **The risk.** Losing Bluefen would knock out about 30% of revenue, which is a value question at the heart of the price.
- **The Seller's position is soft in two ways:**
  - "reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation;
  - deeming the condition satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the clause 11.3 conditions. A consent that still depends on unmet conditions, or that comes with new commercial terms attached, would count as satisfying our condition.
- **Push for:**
  - A condition precedent of unconditional written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably.
  - Evidence that every clause 11.3 condition is satisfied or irrevocably waived.
  - No amendment to the Bluefen contract, and no fee, discount or concession, without Buyer consent.
  - The Seller to use best or all reasonable endeavours, with Buyer involvement in the approach.
  - The condition to be for the Buyer's benefit, so only the Buyer can waive it.
  - A sunset date with a Buyer termination right.
  - A warranty that no notice of termination or non-renewal has been received, plus a pre-completion covenant.
  - Consider a price adjustment or earn-out if Bluefen consents on worse terms.
- **Verify:** whether clause 11.2 is triggered by a share sale (change of control) or only by assignment.

### E. Riverlark facility (DD-003): about AUD 3.2m outstanding

- **The risk.** The clause 8.1 change-control provision will probably be triggered at completion, causing an event of default. A "release to be provided following Completion" is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal. It leaves Riverlark's security over the Company we have just bought, and possibly over the shares themselves.
- **Push for:**
  - A payout letter from Riverlark before completion, confirming the exact payout figure as at the completion date and an undertaking to release on receipt.
  - Repayment at completion out of the purchase price, as a deduction in the funds flow paid directly to Riverlark.
  - Deeds of release delivered at completion.
  - PPSR financing change statements, either lodged or with an irrevocable undertaking to lodge within 1–2 business days.
  - Return of any title documents.
  - The facility (principal, interest, break costs and fees) included in "Debt" for the price calculation.
  - A specific indemnity for any residual Riverlark liability.
- **Verify** through the PPSR and DD-003 whether Riverlark holds a share mortgage or other security over the shares. If so, title cannot pass free of encumbrances without a release at completion.

### F. Completion bonuses (DD-005): AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

- **The problem.** These bonuses are triggered by the transaction and arise because of the Seller's sale. Leaving them out of the funds flow ("a matter for the Seller") actually leaves them with the Company, and therefore with us, after completion.
- **Likely on-costs (verify):**
  - PAYG withholding;
  - NSW payroll tax;
  - superannuation guarantee, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
  - workers' compensation premium effects.
- **Push for:**
  - The full amount, including all employer on-costs, defined as Transaction Costs or Debt and deducted from the price.
  - Payment through Company payroll at or immediately after completion, funded by that deduction.
  - Where bonuses depend on continued employment after completion, the amount held back or put in escrow. Any forfeited amounts should not revert to the Seller unless agreed.
  - A specific indemnity for any shortfall or related tax.
- **Interaction with the basket.** Under the proposed deductible basket of AUD 250k, an on-cost shortfall would likely never be recoverable. That is a good concrete example to use in negotiation.

### G. Ironquay IP (DD-004 / DD-010)

- **The risk.** Clause 7.3 means ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials does not pass to the Company until *every* SOW3 fee is cleared. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. Until that is paid, the Company may not own IP it uses, possibly core product IP. That raises infringement and licence risk, not just a debt. An indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment" covers the 180k and nothing else.
- **Push for:**
  - A completion deliverable or condition requiring the Seller to procure payment of all outstanding SOW3 fees. This should be either a Seller cost or treated as Debt/deducted.
  - Ironquay's written confirmation that all SOW3 fees are paid.
  - A confirmatory deed of assignment of all SOW3 Project Materials and IP, including moral rights consents where relevant.
  - Broadening the indemnity to cover all Loss from the Company not owning, or not having unrestricted rights to, the SOW3 materials, including third-party claims, injunctions, re-development and replacement costs. This should sit outside the general cap and limits.
  - A retention or escrow until the assignment is delivered, if that cannot happen at completion.
- **Verify:** whether other SOW3 fees beyond the 180k exist (the clause says "every SOW3 fee"), and which product components depend on the materials.

### H. Export and privacy incident (DD-006): about 1,240 records

- **The Seller's characterisation is not reliable.** It calls this "preliminary… not expected to be material". The Disclosure Letter itself admits that access, scope and notifiability are unresolved. Business emails, names and roles are personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
- **Timing concern.** Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (Part IIIC), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must take reasonable steps to complete an assessment within 30 days (s 26WH). The investigation was "preliminary" as at 22 September, and it is now 5 November. If no assessment has been completed, the Company may already be non-compliant. That is a regulatory risk in itself, separate from the breach.
- **Customer contract exposure.** Check whether the affected data belongs to Bluefen or other key customers. If so, contractual breach notification and termination rights may be engaged, which compounds the Bluefen risk.
- **Push for:**
  - Immediate disclosure of the full incident file: the timeline, logs, link access records, whether the recipient confirmed deletion, and any legal advice to the extent privilege permits.
  - A pre-signing or pre-completion requirement that the Company completes a documented NDB assessment, with Buyer input. The Company should make any required notifications to the OAIC and individuals, and to customers where contracts require it.
  - A specific indemnity for all Loss arising from the incident: regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, customer claims, notification and remediation costs, forensic costs and credits. This should be uncapped or carry a separate dedicated cap, outside the basket and time limits, with an appropriate survival period.
  - Privacy and data-security warranties that cannot be disclosed against using DD-006.
  - Buyer conduct-of-claims rights after completion.
  - Possibly a retention.

### I. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008 / DD-011): 3 × AUD 110,000

- **Why this needs scrutiny.** The Seller calls these "ordinary-course operating costs". The Disclosure Letter itself says they are "related", should be "read together for timing/scope", and declines to say whether they are ordinary course, terminable or accrued. Three identical renewals of 110k each suggest a single commitment of 330k split up, possibly to stay under an approval or material-contract threshold.
- **Push for:**
  - Full copies and the dates of entry. Check whether they were signed in the lead-up to the sale or during any locked-box or pre-completion period.
  - The reason for splitting the commitment.
  - Their term, termination rights and whether they are prepaid or accrued.
  - Confirmation of whether Sandbar is related to Harbourglass or management.
- **Depending on the answers:**
  - treat the commitment as Debt, leakage or a Transaction Cost;
  - require termination before completion at the Seller's cost;
  - or obtain a specific indemnity.
- **Drafting fix.** Make sure the pre-completion conduct covenants and material-contract thresholds apply to related contracts on an aggregated basis.

### J. Title (DD-012)

- **The problem.** A share register maintained by the Company is weak evidence of title, and the Seller's letter itself declines to vouch for verification.
- **Push for:**
  - Fundamental warranties covering:
    - legal and beneficial ownership;
    - shares fully paid;
    - no encumbrances (see the Riverlark point above);
    - no options, convertibles, SAFEs, ESOP awards, pre-emptive or other rights to shares;
    - the issued capital being exactly as stated.
  - These warranties capped at 100% of price, running 6–7 years, and not able to be disclosed against.
- **Our own checks:** ASIC company extract and historical searches, PPSR search over Harbourglass and the Company, and review of the constitution and any shareholders' agreement for pre-emptive rights and drag provisions.
- **Completion deliverables:**
  - share transfer forms;
  - share certificates, or an indemnity for lost certificates;
  - waivers of pre-emptive rights;
  - board resolutions registering the transfer.

### K. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

Reject this. We should require:

- a standalone **tax indemnity** for pre-completion taxes, including payroll tax and PAYG on the bonuses and any pre-completion transaction taxes;
- tax warranties capped at 100% of price, with the tax limitation period described above;
- IP warranties treated as at least "business-critical", meaning a higher cap and longer time limit, with the Ironquay indemnity sitting separately.

### L. Lower-priority items: verify only

- **Office lease (DD-007).** The Seller says only a notification is required. Verify the clause. Check for change-of-control "deemed assignment" language and any bank guarantee or security deposit in the Seller's or a related entity's name. Make the notification a completion deliverable.
- **Mossvale (DD-009).** The Seller says only an assignment restriction applies. Verify that nothing elsewhere in the contract, such as definitions or termination events, captures a change of control. If anything is ambiguous, seek a waiver or comfort letter before completion.

### M. Seller credit risk (not raised by the Seller, but material)

Harbourglass Ventures appears to be a fund or holding vehicle that will likely distribute the sale proceeds. Our warranty and indemnity rights are only as good as the Seller's ability to pay. **Seek one of the following:**

- a retention or escrow, for example 10–15% for 18 months, plus specific retentions for Ironquay and the incident;
- a parent or fund guarantee;
- buy-side W&I insurance, recognising that W&I will exclude every known issue above. Specific indemnities and escrow are therefore needed either way.

## 4. Known exposures against the proposed package

| Item | Indicative amount | Recoverable under the Seller's draft? |
|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~AUD 3.2m | Not, unless treated as Debt at completion. Disclosed and known, so excluded. |
| Bluefen revenue at risk | ~AUD 3.6m p.a. | Not; disclosed and known. |
| Completion bonuses plus on-costs | AUD 420k + on-costs | Not; disclosed, and falls within the deductible basket. |
| Ironquay SOW3 | AUD 180k + IP risk | Only the 180k payment. |
| Sandbar renewals | AUD 330k | Not; disclosed. |
| DD-006 incident | Unquantified | Not; disclosed. |

## 5. Summary of recommendations

**Process**
1. Reply that the [STANDARD]/[OPEN] categorisation and the "FINAL" status are not accepted, and that all clauses remain open. Confirm internally that no principal-level agreement was given.

**Disclosure and knowledge**

2. Delete general data room and public-register disclosure and replace it with specific, fair disclosure. Allow no disclosure against fundamental, tax or indemnity matters, and no updating between signing and completion.
3. Delete the buyer-knowledge exclusion in cl 8.3 and add an express statement that the Buyer's knowledge does not reduce claims.

**Limitations**

4. Limit the 20% cap and 18-month period to general warranties only. Title and capacity: 100% cap, 6–7 years. Tax: 100% cap, 7 years or the amendment period plus 60 days. Specific indemnities and fraud fall outside the limits.
5. Convert the basket to a tipping basket and lower the de minimis to around AUD 10–15k, aggregating related claims.
6. Carve fraud, specific indemnities, leakage, price adjustment, covenants and equitable relief out of the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5). Narrow non-reliance to statements outside the transaction documents.

**Conditions and completion mechanics**

7. Bluefen: condition precedent of unconditional consent, with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer. The condition is for the Buyer's benefit, with best endeavours, a sunset date and a termination right.
8. Riverlark: payout letter, repayment from the price at completion, deeds of release, PPSR discharges, and the facility included in Debt. Search for any security over the shares.
9. Bonuses: AUD 420k plus all on-costs treated as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted in the funds flow, paid through payroll, and covered by an indemnity.

**Specific indemnities, outside the cap and basket**

10. Ironquay: payment of all SOW3 fees, Ironquay's confirmation, a confirmatory IP assignment as a completion deliverable, and a broad IP indemnity plus retention.
11. DD-006 incident: full incident file now, a completed NDB assessment and any required notifications, and a dedicated indemnity plus retention. Treat the possible delay in the s 26WH assessment as urgent.
12. Sandbar: obtain the full terms and the reasons for splitting the commitment. Then treat it as Debt or leakage, terminate it at the Seller's cost, or obtain an indemnity. Aggregate related contracts in the conduct covenants.

**Title, tax and security for claims**

13. Title: full fundamental share warranties, independent ASIC and PPSR searches, and title deliverables at completion.
14. Tax: standalone tax indemnity, with warranties outside the general regime.
15. Credit support: escrow or retention and/or a fund guarantee, and consider W&I insurance for unknown risks.

**Diligence follow-ups**

16. Confirm the lease and Mossvale positions and verify the Bluefen trigger and any other SOW3 fees.

I can turn this into a mark-up of the Seller's SPA update, a negotiation issues list for the next call, or a short cover reply rejecting the categorisation.

### B. Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5: limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature"

- **Fraud and dishonest concealment.** Limitations must not apply to these. Under NSW law a party generally cannot contract out of liability for its own fraud. Even so, the drafting should say this expressly so there is no argument.
- **Australian Consumer Law s 18.** Misleading or deceptive conduct liability cannot be excluded. However, non-reliance clauses carry evidentiary weight against a reliance case. Limit the non-reliance clause to statements outside the SPA, Disclosure Letter and warranties, and carve out fraud.
- **Exclusive remedy.** This must not cut across:
  - specific indemnities;
  - price adjustment or leakage claims;
  - covenant breaches (pre-completion conduct, restraints);
  - injunctive relief;
  - termination rights.

### C. Disclosure Letter and clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge)

**General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2): reject.** Our position should be:

- Only matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter qualify. Fairly disclosed means with enough detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter, against specific warranties.
- Data room documents are disclosed only if specifically referenced against a warranty. If anything is accepted, take a frozen, indexed copy on USB as an exhibit, not a moving data room.
- Public register disclosure is limited to searches conducted on a stated date, if conceded at all.
- **No disclosure against fundamental warranties or tax**, and none against specific indemnities.
- No updating of the disclosure between signing and completion, or any update gives the Buyer a termination right without curing the breach.

**Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3): reject.** Replace it with a clause stating that the Buyer's knowledge (actual, constructive or imputed), and the Buyer's investigation, do not reduce any claim. The Seller's wording ("the Buyer or its advisers", "discoverable") is especially wide. It would impute to Wattlebridge everything in every adviser's files and everything a search could find. If the Seller holds firm, the fallback is limiting it to the actual knowledge of named individuals, of matters fairly disclosed, as at signing.

**Disclosure Letter 1.4 and 11** (no admission; "Buyer must evaluate"). These are acceptable as reservation language. They also confirm the Seller is not standing behind its characterisations, such as "not expected to be material" and "ordinary course".

### D. Bluefen (DD-002): about AUD 3.6m revenue, around 30% of FY26

- **The risk.** Losing Bluefen would knock out about 30% of revenue, which is a value question at the heart of the price.
- **The Seller's position is soft in two ways:**
  - "reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation;
  - deeming the condition satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the clause 11.3 conditions. A consent that still depends on unmet conditions, or that comes with new commercial terms attached, would count as satisfying our condition.
- **Push for:**
  - A condition precedent of unconditional written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably.
  - Evidence that every clause 11.3 condition is satisfied or irrevocably waived.
  - No amendment to the Bluefen contract, and no fee, discount or concession, without Buyer consent.
  - The Seller to use best or all reasonable endeavours, with Buyer involvement in the approach.
  - The condition to be for the Buyer's benefit, so only the Buyer can waive it.
  - A sunset date with a Buyer termination right.
  - A warranty that no notice of termination or non-renewal has been received, plus a pre-completion covenant.
  - Consider a price adjustment or earn-out if Bluefen consents on worse terms.
- **Verify:** whether clause 11.2 is triggered by a share sale (change of control) or only by assignment.

### E. Riverlark facility (DD-003): about AUD 3.2m outstanding

- **The risk.** The clause 8.1 change-control provision will probably be triggered at completion, causing an event of default. A "release to be provided following Completion" is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal. It leaves Riverlark's security over the Company we have just bought, and possibly over the shares themselves.

### F. Completion bonuses (DD-005): AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

- **The problem.** These bonuses are triggered by the transaction and arise because of the Seller's sale. Leaving them out of the funds flow ("a matter for the Seller") actually leaves them with the Company, and therefore with us, after completion.

### G. Ironquay IP (DD-004 / DD-010)

- **The risk.** Clause 7.3 means ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials does not pass to the Company until *every* SOW3 fee is cleared. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. Until that is paid, the Company may not own IP it uses, possibly core product IP. That raises infringement and licence risk, not just a debt. An indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment" covers the 180k and nothing else.
- **Push for:**
  - A completion deliverable or condition requiring the Seller to procure payment of all outstanding SOW3 fees. This should be either a Seller cost or treated as Debt/deducted.
  - Ironquay's written confirmation that all SOW3 fees are paid.
  - A confirmatory deed of assignment of all SOW3 Project Materials and IP, including moral rights consents where relevant.
  - Broadening the indemnity to cover all Loss from the Company not owning, or not having unrestricted rights to, the SOW3 materials, including third-party claims, injunctions, re-development and replacement costs. This should sit outside the general cap and limits.

### H. Export and privacy incident (DD-006): about 1,240 records

- **The Seller's characterisation is not reliable.** It calls this "preliminary… not expected to be material". The Disclosure Letter itself admits that access, scope and notifiability are unresolved. Business emails, names and roles are personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
- **Timing concern.** Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (Part IIIC), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must take reasonable steps to complete an assessment within 30 days (s 26WH). The investigation was "preliminary" as at 22 September, and it is now 5 November. If no assessment has been completed, the Company may already be non-compliant. That is a regulatory risk in itself, separate from the breach.
- **Customer contract exposure.** Check whether the affected data belongs to Bluefen or other key customers. If so, contractual breach notification and termination rights may be engaged, which compounds the Bluefen risk.
- **Push for:**
  - Immediate disclosure of the full incident file: the timeline, logs, link access records, whether the recipient confirmed deletion, and any legal advice to the extent privilege permits.
  - A pre-signing or pre-completion requirement that the Company completes a documented NDB assessment, with Buyer input. The Company should make any required notifications to the OAIC and individuals, and to customers where contracts require it.
  - A specific indemnity for all Loss arising from the incident: regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, customer claims, notification and remediation costs, forensic costs and credits. This should be uncapped or carry a separate dedicated cap, outside the basket and time limits, with an appropriate survival period.
  - Privacy and data-security warranties that cannot be disclosed against using DD-006.
  - Buyer conduct-of-claims rights after completion.
  - Possibly a retention.

### I. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008 / DD-011): 3 × AUD 110,000

- **Why this needs scrutiny.** The Seller calls these "ordinary-course operating costs". The Disclosure Letter itself says they are "related", should be "read together for timing/scope", and declines to say whether they are ordinary course, terminable or accrued. Three identical renewals of 110k each suggest a single commitment of 330k split up, possibly to stay under an approval or material-contract threshold.

### J. Title (DD-012)

- **The problem.** A share register maintained by the Company is weak evidence of title, and the Seller's letter itself declines to vouch for verification.
- **Push for:**

    - shares fully paid;

Reject this. We should require:

- **Office lease (DD-007).** The Seller says only a notification is required. Verify the clause. Check for change-of-control "deemed assignment" language and any bank guarantee or security deposit in the Seller's or a related entity's name. Make the notification a completion deliverable.

### M. Seller credit risk (not raised by the Seller, but material)

Harbourglass Ventures appears to be a fund or holding vehicle that will likely distribute the sale proceeds. Our warranty and indemnity rights are only as good as the Seller's ability to pay. **Seek one of the following:**

- a retention or escrow, for example 10–15% for 18 months, plus specific retentions for Ironquay and the incident;
- a parent or fund guarantee;
- buy-side W&I insurance, recognising that W&I will exclude every known issue above. Specific indemnities and escrow are therefore needed either way.

## 5. Summary of recommendations

**Process**
1. Reply that the [STANDARD]/[OPEN] categorisation and the "FINAL" status are not accepted, and that all clauses remain open. Confirm internally that no principal-level agreement was given.

**Disclosure and knowledge**

2. Delete general data room and public-register disclosure and replace it with specific, fair disclosure. Allow no disclosure against fundamental, tax or indemnity matters, and no updating between signing and completion.
3. Delete the buyer-knowledge exclusion in cl 8.3 and add an express statement that the Buyer's knowledge does not reduce claims.

**Limitations**

4. Limit the 20% cap and 18-month period to general warranties only. Title and capacity: 100% cap, 6–7 years. Tax: 100% cap, 7 years or the amendment period plus 60 days. Specific indemnities and fraud fall outside the limits.
5. Convert the basket to a tipping basket and lower the de minimis to around AUD 10–15k, aggregating related claims.
6. Carve fraud, specific indemnities, leakage, price adjustment, covenants and equitable relief out of the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5). Narrow non-reliance to statements outside the transaction documents.

**Conditions and completion mechanics**

7. Bluefen: condition precedent of unconditional consent, with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer. The condition is for the Buyer's benefit, with best endeavours, a sunset date and a termination right.
8. Riverlark: payout letter, repayment from the price at completion, deeds of release, PPSR discharges, and the facility included in Debt. Search for any security over the shares.
9. Bonuses: AUD 420k plus all on-costs treated as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted in the funds flow, paid through payroll, and covered by an indemnity.

**Specific indemnities, outside the cap and basket**

10. Ironquay: payment of all SOW3 fees, Ironquay's confirmation, a confirmatory IP assignment as a completion deliverable, and a broad IP indemnity plus retention.
11. DD-006 incident: full incident file now, a completed NDB assessment and any required notifications, and a dedicated indemnity plus retention. Treat the possible delay in the s 26WH assessment as urgent.
12. Sandbar: obtain the full terms and the reasons for splitting the commitment. Then treat it as Debt or leakage, terminate it at the Seller's cost, or obtain an indemnity. Aggregate related contracts in the conduct covenants.

**Title, tax and security for claims**

13. Title: full fundamental share warranties, independent ASIC and PPSR searches, and title deliverables at completion.
14. Tax: standalone tax indemnity, with warranties outside the general regime.
15. Credit support: escrow or retention and/or a fund guarantee, and consider W&I insurance for unknown risks.

16. Confirm the lease and Mossvale positions and verify the Bluefen trigger and any other SOW3 fees.
